opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few categories that seem pretty promising to me, though I'd caveat that I'm mostly a technical person, so take my views on the policy side with some salt.

One thing that seems really valuable is just improving transparency into what's going on at AI companies. Right now, a lot of the most important information, like what capabilities models actually have internally, what safety measures are actually in place, and how close companies think they are to really transformative systems, isn't very visible to the outside world. Things like requiring companies to publish their safety policies, report on how they're actually following them, and disclose serious incidents seem quite good and relatively cheap. Whistleblower protections fit in here too: if an employee sees something going badly wrong, it should be easy and safe for them to raise it.

A second category is getting governments, especially the US government, more situationally aware. I think there's a decent chance things move very fast, possibly with AI substantially automating AI research itself, and if that happens, you'd really want people in government who understand what's going on and have thought ahead about how to respond. So building capacity there, with people who are technically literate and take the possibility of very rapid progress seriously, seems helpful even if you're unsure exactly which policies you'd want.

Third, security. I'd count this as partially nontechnical because so much of it is about institutional will and resources. If model weights for very powerful systems get stolen, a lot of other safety efforts get undermined. Pushing companies toward much stronger security, and getting governments to help with that, seems robustly good.

Then there's the broader question of coordination: things that would let developers slow down at critical points rather than being forced to race. I'm more uncertain about what's tractable there. International agreements seem hard, but even laying groundwork, like getting verification ideas worked out in advance, could matter a lot if political will appears suddenly after some warning shot.

And finally, I think just getting more good people working on this, inside companies, in government, and in nonprofits, is a big lever. A lot of my optimism about any particular scenario routes through whether there are a handful of competent, well-informed people in the right places when key decisions get made.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transparency, security, government capacity, and coordination, but does not identify human power grabs as an AI risk beyond misalignment.

r002.rationale: It calls for technically literate people in government, but does not say technical AI safety work should be translated into terms policymakers can use.

r003.rationale: The response mentions verification ideas for international coordination, but not compute governance, verification of AI training claims, or US–China coordination.

r004.rationale: It recommends building government capacity with technically literate people who take rapid AI progress seriously and have thought ahead about how to respond.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention bioweapons defenses or connect them to AI takeover scenarios.

r006.rationale: It recommends stronger security against model-weight theft, but does not state that defensive investments against AI-enabled threats are worthwhile even without misalignment risk.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's actually a lot here, and in some ways I've become more optimistic about the nontechnical side relative to where I was a few years ago. Let me try to break it into a few buckets.

The first thing I'd point to is just transparency and information. A huge fraction of what makes me worried about how things go is that key decisions get made by a small number of people inside labs, under time pressure, with information the rest of the world doesn't have. So things like: AI companies publicly stating what their safety policies are, committing to disclose when they've trained a model above some capability threshold, reporting on what internal evals showed, having whistleblower protections so employees can flag when a company is deviating from what it said it would do. None of that requires solving alignment. It just makes it harder for a company to quietly cut corners, and it gives external actors — governments, other labs, the public — the ability to respond. I think transparency regimes are among the highest-value, lowest-cost things on the table, and they're also the kind of thing that's relatively easy to get agreement on because they don't directly stop anyone from doing anything.

A second bucket is getting the right people and the right norms into positions that matter. By that I mean people who take the risks seriously working in government, on policy teams at labs, on the boards and oversight bodies of these companies. A lot of what determines how a crunch moment goes is just who's in the room and what they think is reasonable. I'd also put things like building a shared understanding across labs about what counts as a red line — what evidence would make you pause — in this category. Even if there's no formal enforcement, having the leading labs roughly agree on "if we see X, we stop and coordinate" is meaningfully better than each lab improvising.

Third, and this is the one I think people underweight, is just slowing things down at the critical moment and having the option to do so. A lot of my model of how things go badly involves a very rapid takeoff — AIs automating AI R&D, capabilities going from "roughly human expert" to "far beyond" over a period of months. In that world, the technical safety work you have time to do is basically fixed by how much calendar time you have. So anything that buys time — regulation that requires some kind of review before deploying or training frontier systems, agreements between labs or between countries not to race, compute governance that makes it possible to actually verify what people are doing — those are all extremely valuable even if they're not themselves "safety research." I'd say international coordination on compute is maybe the single most leveraged nontechnical thing, though it's also hard. If the US and China could agree on some kind of monitoring of the largest training runs, that changes the game a lot. I'm not confident that's achievable, but the payoff is high enough that it's worth a lot of effort.

Fourth is what I'd call preparedness and incident response. Having governments that actually understand what's going on — technical staff, the ability to run their own evaluations, relationships with the labs so that if something alarming happens there's a channel to escalate it. Right now, if a lab discovered strong evidence that a model was deceptively aligned, it's not obvious who they'd call or what would happen next. Just having that infrastructure exist seems valuable.

And then I'd mention something a bit more philosophical, which is advocacy and shifting the general conversation. I've gone back and forth on this. There's a version of it that I think is bad — making exaggerated claims, polarizing things. But I do think it matters that a decent chunk of the public and of policymakers treat "we might build systems smarter than us and lose control" as a serious possibility rather than a sci-fi thing. That shapes what's politically feasible on all the other items. Credible researchers being willing to say publicly what they actually believe about the risk, even when it's uncomfortable, seems good to me.

If I had to rank, I'd say the transparency stuff and the "buy time at the critical moment" stuff are the ones I'd most want to see more effort on. They're relatively robust across different views of how AI development goes. Even if you think alignment turns out to be easy, having better information and more time doesn't hurt much. And if it turns out to be hard, they're a huge deal.

r006.rationale: It says transparency and more time could help even if alignment is easy, but does not identify defensive investments against AI-enabled threats as worthwhile absent misalignment risk.

astra-6.text:
I’d probably put the most weight on governance that helps us notice when systems are becoming dangerous and then actually do something about it. That includes getting governments better information about what frontier labs are building, having credible evaluations of dangerous capabilities, and making sure there’s some ability to delay deployment or further development if the evidence looks concerning.

One distinction I’d make is between having a policy written down and having an institution that can implement it well. You need people who understand the technology, can scrutinise the evidence, and have enough authority to act. Building that capacity seems valuable across a fairly wide range of views about how AI will develop.

Security also seems important: reducing the chance that powerful model weights get stolen, for example. Technical safeguards are part of that, but organisational practices and government policy matter too.

I’m less confident about which particular political strategy is best. A lot depends on what’s feasible and what the relevant actors would otherwise do. But broadly, improving visibility into frontier development and creating a credible mechanism for responding to serious risks seem like promising places to focus.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one promising approach is trying to make sure that, before companies deploy really powerful systems, there’s a credible process for assessing whether those systems pose catastrophic risks—and that the results actually affect deployment decisions. That includes technical evaluations, but a lot of the work is institutional: who gets access to the model, who can scrutinize the evidence, and whether anyone has the authority to say, “We need to stop or slow down here.”

Another important area is security. If a company develops a very powerful model, preventing its weights from being stolen could matter a lot. That’s partly a technical problem, but it also involves organizational competence, incentives, and government coordination.

More broadly, I’d like policymakers to have better information and more capacity to respond as the situation changes. I’m somewhat more confident in measures that give us visibility and preserve the ability to act than in a very detailed regulatory framework that assumes we already know exactly what the dangerous systems will look like.

The caveat is that implementation matters enormously. A policy can sound sensible and then turn into a box-checking exercise. So I’d focus on whether a particular intervention actually changes what happens when there’s evidence of serious danger.
